#### VDM-001: Domain registered through Vercel is about to lapse

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Domains · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/renew-a-domain)

Auto-renew is off and the registration ends soon. A lapsed domain stops resolving, and anyone can register it afterwards and receive your traffic and email.

**How to fix**

Turn on auto-renew for the domain under Domains, or renew it now. Check the payment method on file.

#### VDM-002: Project domain isn't verified

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Project domains · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting#domain-verification)

Vercel couldn't confirm you own the domain, usually because another team or account uses it. Until it's verified, it doesn't serve this project, and someone else may control it.

**How to fix**

Add the TXT record Vercel shows under the project's Settings → Domains, or remove the domain if it isn't yours.

### Vercel: Platform

#### VPL-001: Functions run on a Node.js version past end of life

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Projects · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js/node-js-versions)

Node.js gets no security fixes after its end-of-life date, and Vercel stops building on old versions without much notice.

**How to fix**

Choose a supported Node.js version under the project's Settings → Build and Deployment → Node.js Version, then redeploy and test.

#### VPL-002: Directory listing is on

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Projects · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/directory-listing)

Visitors can browse every file in a folder without an index page, which can reveal backups, configuration and files that were never linked.

**How to fix**

Turn off Settings → Advanced → Directory Listing.

#### VPL-003: Source maps are public

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Projects · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-protection/protecting-sourcemaps)

Public source maps hand anyone your original source code, comments included, which makes finding weaknesses much easier.

**How to fix**

Turn on Protected Source Maps under Settings → Deployment Protection.

#### VPL-006: Production hasn't been redeployed in over a year

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Projects · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/deployments/managing-deployments#redeploy-a-project)

Dependency fixes, framework security releases and runtime patches only reach a site when it's rebuilt. A year-old production build carries every vulnerability found since.

**How to fix**

Update the project's dependencies and redeploy, or, if the site is no longer needed, remove its domains and delete the project.

### Vercel: Monitoring

#### VMN-001: Logs aren't kept outside Vercel

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Drains · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/drains)

Vercel keeps runtime logs for a short time. Without a drain, there's nothing to search after an incident that's more than a few days old.

**How to fix**

Add a log drain to your log platform or an S3 bucket under Team Settings → Drains.

#### VMN-002: Drain writes logs to S3 as public objects

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Drains · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/drains)

The drain sets a public ACL on every object it writes, so anyone with an object's URL can read request logs, which hold IP addresses, paths and sometimes tokens.

**How to fix**

Change the drain's object ACL to private or bucket-owner-full-control, then remove public access from the objects already written.

#### VMN-003: Logs or webhooks are sent without encryption

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Drains, Webhooks · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/drains)

An http:// endpoint sends logs or event payloads in clear text, where anyone on the path can read or change them.

**How to fix**

Change the endpoint to https:// under Team Settings → Drains or Webhooks.

#### VMN-004: Drain is disabled or failing

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Drains · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/drains)

Logs stopped reaching their destination, so alerts and investigations that rely on them see nothing.

**How to fix**

Open the drain under Team Settings → Drains, fix the endpoint or credentials, and turn it back on.

### Vercel: Change risk

#### VPL-005: Project isn't connected to Git

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Projects · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/git)

Deployments come from someone's machine through the CLI, so there's no review, no history of what was deployed and no easy rollback to a known commit.

**How to fix**

Connect the repository under Settings → Git, and deploy through pull requests.

## AWS

### AWS: Attack surface

#### ANW-004: Transit gateway joins shared VPCs without approval

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Transit gateways · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-transit-gateways.html#tgw-modifying)

Any account the transit gateway is shared with can attach a VPC and reach the networks behind it, without anyone in this account accepting it.

**How to fix**

In VPC → Transit gateways → the gateway → Modify, untick Auto accept shared attachments, and accept each attachment by hand.

#### AS3-001: S3 Block Public Access is off for the account

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** S3 Block Public Access for the account, S3 buckets · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/configuring-block-public-access-account.html)

Without the account-wide block, any bucket can be made public by one policy or ACL change, now or later. With it on, a mistake on a single bucket can't expose data.

**How to fix**

In the S3 console → Block Public Access settings for this account, turn on all four settings. Buckets that must be public (a static site, for example) are better served through CloudFront.

#### AS3-002: S3 bucket is public

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** S3 Block Public Access for the account, S3 buckets, S3 bucket access settings · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

Anyone on the internet can read the bucket, and with some policies list or write to it. Public buckets are the most common source of leaked data on AWS.

**How to fix**

1. If the bucket shouldn't be public, open it in S3 → Permissions and turn on Block Public Access.
2. Then remove the public statement from its policy and the public grants from its ACL.
3. If it serves a website through CloudFront, edit the distribution's origin to use origin access control, let CloudFront add the bucket policy it offers, and then turn on Block Public Access.

#### AS3-003: S3 bucket has no Block Public Access of its own

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** S3 Block Public Access for the account, S3 buckets, S3 bucket access settings · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

The bucket is private today, but neither it nor the account blocks public access, so one policy or ACL change makes it public.

**How to fix**

Open the bucket in S3 → Permissions → Block public access and turn on all four settings, or turn the block on for the whole account.

#### ANW-001: Security group opens SSH or RDP to the internet

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Security groups, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html)

Remote administration ports are scanned and brute-forced around the clock. An exposed SSH or RDP port turns one weak password or unpatched service into a foothold.

**How to fix**

1. Edit the group's inbound rules and replace 0.0.0.0/0 with your office or VPN range.
2. Better: remove the rule and connect with Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, which need no inbound port.
3. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### ANW-002: Security group opens a database port to the internet

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Security groups, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html)

A database reachable from the internet is protected by its password alone, and exposed to every bug in its network protocol.

**How to fix**

Edit the group's inbound rules so the database port is allowed only from the security group of the application that uses it, not from 0.0.0.0/0. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### ANW-003: Security group allows all traffic from the internet

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Security groups, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html)

Every port of everything that uses this group is reachable by anyone: admin interfaces, databases, debug ports and services nobody remembers are listening.

**How to fix**

Edit the group's inbound rules: delete the rule that allows all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, and add rules for the specific ports the service needs. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### AEC-003: EBS snapshot is public

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** EBS encryption, public snapshots and public images · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-modifying-snapshot-permissions.html)

Any AWS account can copy the snapshot and mount it: the whole disk, with whatever databases, keys and configuration were on it.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Snapshots, select the snapshot → Actions → Modify permissions, and set it to Private. Treat every secret that was on the disk as leaked and rotate it.

#### AEC-004: Machine image (AMI) is public

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** EBS encryption, public snapshots and public images · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/sharingamis-intro.html)

Any AWS account can launch the image and read what was baked into it: application code, configuration, and often credentials.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → AMIs, select the image → Actions → Edit AMI permissions, and set it to Private. If it was meant to be shared, share it with specific accounts instead.

#### AEC-006: Lambda function URL needs no authentication

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Lambda functions and function URLs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/urls-auth.html)

Anyone who finds the URL can invoke the function. Unless the function checks callers itself, they can use whatever it does and run up its bill.

**How to fix**

If the function isn't a public endpoint, set its function URL's auth type to AWS_IAM under Lambda → the function → Configuration → Function URL. If it is public on purpose and checks requests itself, mark this as accepted.

#### AEC-012: Snapshots and machine images can still be made public

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Blocks on sharing snapshots and images publicly · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/block-public-access-snapshots.html)

Anyone in the account who can change a snapshot's or image's permissions can share it with everyone, and with it the data on its disks. A block on public sharing stops that for the whole region.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Settings → Data protection and security, turn on Block public access for EBS snapshots (Block all public sharing) and for AMIs.

#### AEC-013: Lambda function's policy lets anyone invoke it

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Lambda functions and function URLs, Lambda function policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/access-control-resource-based.html)

Its resource policy allows any AWS account, or anyone, to call it without a condition. They can run it with whatever input they choose, as its role, and on your bill.

**How to fix**

In Lambda → the function → Configuration → Permissions → Resource-based policy statements, remove the statement for "*", or add a condition that names the source (aws:SourceArn or aws:SourceAccount).

#### AEC-015: SageMaker notebook has direct internet access

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** SageMaker notebook instances · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/appendix-notebook-and-internet-access.html)

The notebook can reach anywhere on the internet outside your VPC's controls, so code or data in it can leave without passing any firewall or log you run.

**How to fix**

Notebook instances can't change this in place: create a new one in a VPC subnet with Direct internet access disabled, give it a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for what it needs, and move the work over.

#### ACN-001: EKS API endpoint is open to the whole internet

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** EKS clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/cluster-endpoint.html)

Anyone can reach the cluster's Kubernetes API. One leaked kubeconfig, token or API vulnerability is then enough to control the workloads, without being on your network.

**How to fix**

In EKS → the cluster → Networking → Manage endpoint access, turn on private access, and either turn public access off or limit it to your offices' and CI's address ranges.

#### ACN-006: ECR repository is public

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/repository-policies.html)

Its repository policy lets anyone pull images, and with them any code, configuration or secrets built into them. If it also allows pushing, anyone can replace the images your services run.

**How to fix**

In ECR → the repository → Permissions, remove the statement for "*" or name the accounts and roles that need access. Use ECR Public for images meant to be public.

#### ADB-001: Database is publicly accessible

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** RDS databases, Security groups · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_VPC.WorkingWithRDSInstanceinaVPC.html#USER_VPC.Hiding)

The database has a public address. Only its security group and its password keep the internet out, and one loosened rule exposes it.

**How to fix**

1. In RDS → the database → Modify → Connectivity → Additional configuration, choose Not publicly accessible.
2. Reach it from inside the VPC, through a VPN, or with Session Manager port forwarding.

#### ADB-004: Database snapshot is public

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** RDS manual snapshots and who may restore them · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ShareSnapshot.html)

Any AWS account can restore the snapshot and read the whole database as it was, with no password and nothing in your logs.

**How to fix**

In RDS → Snapshots → Manual → the snapshot → Actions → Share snapshot, set DB snapshot visibility to Private. If it may already have been copied, treat its data and credentials as exposed.

#### ADB-006: OpenSearch domain is open to anyone

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** OpenSearch domains · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/ac.html)

The domain has a public endpoint and an access policy that lets anyone in, so anyone who finds it can search, change and delete its indexes.

**How to fix**

1. Replace the access policy with one that names your IAM roles or address ranges.
2. Turn on fine-grained access control.
3. Better, move the domain into a VPC: create a new one with VPC access and restore a snapshot into it.

#### ADB-011: Redshift cluster is publicly accessible

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Redshift clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/managing-clusters-vpc.html)

The data warehouse has a public address. Only its security group and passwords stand between the internet and your data.

**How to fix**

In Redshift → the cluster → Actions → Modify publicly accessible setting, turn it off, and reach the cluster from inside the VPC or through a VPN.

#### ASC-007: Systems Manager document is shared with everyone

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Systems Manager documents and who they're shared with · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/documents-ssm-sharing.html)

Any AWS account can read the document, and with it the commands, script paths, hostnames and sometimes credentials it holds.

**How to fix**

In Systems Manager → Documents → Owned by me → the document → Permissions, choose Private, and share with named accounts only. The account setting Block public sharing stops it happening again.

#### ASC-009: CodeBuild project's builds are public

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** CodeBuild projects (environment variables scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/public-builds.html)

Anyone on the internet can read the project's build logs and artifacts, which often show paths, versions, hostnames and the output of every command.

**How to fix**

In CodeBuild → the project → Edit → Project configuration, set Public build access off.

#### AMQ-001: SNS topic lets anyone publish or subscribe

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** SNS topics, their policies and subscriptions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-access-policy-use-cases.html)

The topic policy allows "*" without a condition, so any AWS account can send messages to everything subscribed, or subscribe and receive what you publish.

**How to fix**

In SNS → the topic → Access policy, remove the statement for "*" or add a condition that names the source (aws:SourceAccount, aws:SourceArn) or your organization (aws:PrincipalOrgID).

#### AMQ-003: SQS queue lets anyone send or read messages

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** SQS queues and their policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-basic-examples-of-sqs-policies.html)

The queue policy allows "*" without a condition, so any AWS account can put messages your consumers will act on, or read and delete the ones meant for them.

**How to fix**

In SQS → the queue → Access policy, remove the statement for "*" or add a condition (aws:SourceArn for an SNS topic or S3 bucket, aws:PrincipalOrgID for your organization).

#### AMQ-004: Amazon MQ broker is publicly accessible

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Amazon MQ brokers · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazon-mq/latest/developer-guide/amazon-mq-security.html)

The broker and its web console have public addresses, so only its users' passwords keep the internet from your messages.

**How to fix**

Public accessibility can't be changed in place: create a private broker in your VPC, move producers and consumers to it, and delete the public one.

#### AMQ-005: Kafka cluster accepts unauthenticated or unencrypted clients

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** MSK (Kafka) clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/msk/latest/developerguide/msk-authentication.html)

Clients can connect without proving who they are, or in plain text, so anyone who reaches the brokers can read and write every topic, or watch the traffic.

**How to fix**

In MSK → the cluster → Properties → Security settings, turn on IAM, SASL/SCRAM or TLS client authentication and turn off unauthenticated access; set encryption between clients and brokers to TLS only. Turn off public access unless clients outside AWS need it.

#### AMQ-006: EventBridge event bus accepts events from any account

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** EventBridge event buses · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-event-bus-perms.html)

The bus policy allows "*" without a condition, so any AWS account can put events that your rules then act on: start workflows, invoke functions, send notifications.

**How to fix**

In EventBridge → Event buses → the bus → Permissions, name the accounts that may send events, or add an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition for your organization.

#### AED-009: Load balancer passes ambiguous HTTP requests to its targets

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/application-load-balancers.html#desync-mitigation-mode)

Desync mitigation is in monitor mode, so requests that the load balancer and the application could read differently are passed on. That is how HTTP request smuggling slips requests past the load balancer's rules.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Load Balancers → the load balancer → Attributes → Edit, set Desync mitigation mode to Defensive (the default) or Strictest.

#### AED-010: CloudFront serves from an S3 bucket that doesn't exist

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html)

The distribution's origin is a bucket nobody owns. Anyone can create a bucket with that name in their own account and serve their content on your distribution's hostnames.

**How to fix**

Create the bucket in this account now so the name is yours, then point the origin at the bucket that should serve the content, or remove the origin and its behaviours.

### AWS: Identity & access

#### AID-001: Root user has no MFA

**Severity:** Critical · **Reads:** IAM account summary (root user) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/enable-mfa-for-root.html)

The root user can do anything in the account, including closing it, and no policy can restrict it. With a password alone, one phished or reused password gives all of that away.

**How to fix**

1. Sign in as the root user.
2. Open the account menu → Security credentials.
3. Under Multi-factor authentication, assign a passkey or hardware key, and keep a second one somewhere safe.

#### AID-002: Root user has access keys

**Severity:** Critical · **Reads:** IAM account summary (root user) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

A root access key is a permanent credential with full control of the account that MFA doesn't protect and no policy can limit. If it leaks from a laptop, a script or a repository, the account is gone.

**How to fix**

1. Find what uses the key and move it to an IAM role or a user with only the permissions it needs.
2. Sign in as the root user → Security credentials → Access keys, and delete the key.

#### AID-003: IAM user can sign in to the console without MFA

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa_enable.html)

The user's password is all that stands between an attacker and everything the user can do in the console.

**How to fix**

Open the user in IAM → Security credentials → Multi-factor authentication and assign a device. If the person signs in through IAM Identity Center instead, remove the console password.

#### AID-004: Access key is older than 90 days

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id-credentials-access-keys-update.html)

Access keys never expire on their own. The longer one lives, the more places it has been copied to, and the more likely one of them leaks.

**How to fix**

1. Create a second key for the user.
2. Switch the system that uses the old key over.
3. Deactivate the old key, and delete it once nothing breaks. Better: replace the user with an IAM role.

#### AID-005: Access key unused for 90 days

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_finding-unused.html)

A key nobody uses is access nobody needs, and nobody will notice when someone else starts using it.

**How to fix**

Open the user in IAM → Security credentials, deactivate the key, and delete it after a few weeks without complaints.

#### AID-006: Console password unused for 90 days

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_finding-unused.html)

The person has left, changed role, or signs in another way, but their password still works.

**How to fix**

Open the user in IAM → Security credentials → Console sign-in and remove console access, or delete the user if nothing else uses it.

#### AID-007: Password policy is missing or weak

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM password policy, IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_passwords_account-policy.html)

IAM users with console passwords can pick short passwords and reuse old ones, which makes guessing and credential stuffing work.

**How to fix**

In IAM → Account settings → Password policy, require at least 14 characters and prevent password reuse.

#### AID-008: Administrator has a long-lived access key

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** IAM users, their access keys and MFA devices, IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#bp-users-federation-idp)

The key gives full control of the account to whoever holds it, without MFA and without an expiry. Keys leak from laptops, CI logs and repositories far more often than passwords do.

**How to fix**

1. Move the workload to an IAM role, or give its user only the permissions it needs.
2. For people, use IAM Identity Center or a role assumed with MFA.
3. Delete the administrator's access key.

#### AID-009: IAM role can be assumed by any AWS account

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html)

The role's trust policy names every AWS principal, with no condition. Anyone with an AWS account can assume the role and use its permissions.

**How to fix**

Open the role in IAM → Trust relationships and replace the wildcard principal with the specific account, role or service that needs it. For a third party, also require an external ID.

#### AID-010: Customer managed policy allows every action on every resource

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#grant-least-privilege)

The policy is a second AdministratorAccess under another name. Whoever it is attached to is an administrator, which reviews that look for AdministratorAccess will miss.

**How to fix**

Open the policy in IAM → Policies and narrow its actions and resources to what its users need, or detach it and use AdministratorAccess where full access is intended.

#### AID-011: IAM role trusts an AWS account outside the entity without an external ID

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html)

Another company's AWS account can assume this role with nothing but its own permissions. If that account is a vendor's, any of the vendor's other customers may be able to make it act on your account (the confused deputy problem); if it is an old partner or a forgotten account, it still has the access.

**How to fix**

1. Open the role in IAM → Trust relationships.
2. If the other account is one of yours, add it to this entity in Keelson.
3. If it is a vendor's, add a Condition that requires the external ID they gave you (sts:ExternalId).
4. If nobody uses the role any more, delete it.

#### AID-013: IAM identity can give itself more access

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_manage-edit.html)

Its policies aren't administrator access, but they let it get there: change or attach a policy, create keys or passwords for other users, or hand a stronger role to an instance or function it starts. Whoever holds its credentials can take over the account.

**How to fix**

1. Open the policy named in the finding.
2. Remove the IAM actions listed, or limit them to named resources (Resource with an ARN, not "*").
3. For iam:PassRole, name the roles it may pass and add an iam:PassedToService condition.

#### AID-014: Cognito identity pool gives AWS credentials to anyone

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Cognito user pools and identity pools · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/identity-pools.html#authenticated-and-unauthenticated-identities)

Guest access is on, so anyone on the internet can get temporary AWS credentials for the pool's guest role, without signing in. Whatever that role may do, they can do.

**How to fix**

In Cognito → Identity pools → the pool → User access, turn off Guest access. If guests need it, give the guest role only the few actions they need, on named resources.

#### AID-015: Cognito user pool doesn't offer multi-factor sign-in

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Cognito user pools and identity pools · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/user-pool-settings-mfa.html)

Users can only sign in with a password, so a reused or phished password is enough to take over their account in your application.

**How to fix**

In Cognito → User pools → the pool → Authentication methods → Multi-factor authentication, choose Optional MFA (or Require MFA for staff-only pools) and turn on authenticator apps.

#### AS3-004: Bucket policy lets an AWS account outside the entity in

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** S3 bucket policies (reduced to the accounts they allow, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-walkthroughs-managing-access-example2.html)

Another AWS account can read or write the bucket with its own credentials. If it belongs to a former vendor or partner, or was never yours, it keeps that access, and you see none of its activity in your own logs.

**How to fix**

1. Open the bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy.
2. If the account is one of yours, add it to this entity in Keelson.
3. Otherwise remove the statement that names it, or narrow it to the objects and actions it needs.

#### AEC-007: Internet-facing instance runs with administrator access

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** EC2 instances, Security groups, IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html)

The instance has a public address and open ports, and the role attached to it can do anything in the account. One vulnerability in whatever listens there (a web app, an SSH daemon, an exposed admin tool) hands the attacker the role's credentials, and with them the account.

**How to fix**

1. Give the instance a role with only the permissions its software uses. IAM Access Analyzer can generate one from the role's CloudTrail activity.
2. Require IMDSv2 on the instance.
3. Put it behind a load balancer and close its public ports, or remove its public address.

#### AID-012: GitHub Actions in any repository can assume this IAM role

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-idp_oidc.html#idp_oidc_Create_GitHub)

The role trusts GitHub's OIDC provider without limiting the token's subject to your repositories. A workflow in anyone's repository, on any GitHub account, can get a token GitHub signs and assume the role.

**How to fix**

Open the role in IAM → Trust relationships and add a condition on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub naming your organization and repository, for example repo:your-org/your-repo:ref:refs/heads/main or repo:your-org/your-repo:environment:production.

#### XP-010: IAM role trusts GitHub repositories outside the entity

**Severity:** High · **Spans providers** · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect)

GitHub Actions in a GitHub organization that isn't one of the entity's can assume this role. That organization's members, and anyone who gets write access to its repositories, get the role's AWS access.

**How to fix**

1. If the organization is yours, add it to this entity in Keelson.
2. If it belongs to a vendor, confirm they still need the role and limit it to the repository and branch they use.
3. Otherwise remove it from the role's trust policy.

#### XP-011: Anyone who can push to the repository can assume this IAM role

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Spans providers** · **Reads:** IAM roles, groups and policies · [GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect#example-subject-claims)

The role trusts GitHub Actions from a repository in the entity, either from any branch or pull request, or from a default branch that takes changes without review. Anyone with write access, or a stolen token or deploy key that has it, can push a workflow and act as the role in AWS.

**How to fix**

1. Limit the trust policy's subject to the protected default branch (repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main) or, better, to a GitHub environment with required reviewers (repo:org/repo:environment:production).
2. Require a reviewed pull request on that branch in GitHub.

### AWS: Secrets

#### AEC-008: Credential in an instance's start-up script

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Instance start-up scripts (scanned for credentials, never stored), EC2 instances · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/user-data.html)

User data isn't a secret store: anyone who can describe the instance can read it, every process on the instance can fetch it from the metadata service, and it is copied into launch templates and images. A credential written there is readable far beyond the people who should have it.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential: treat it as leaked.
2. Move it to Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, and let the script read it at start-up with the instance's role.
3. Replace the instance (or its launch template) so the old script is gone.

#### AEC-010: Credential in a launch template's start-up script

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** EC2 launch templates (start-up scripts scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/user-data.html)

Anyone who can describe launch templates or reach an instance's metadata can read the start-up script, and the credential written into it. It also lands on every instance started from the template.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential.
2. Create a new template version that reads it at start-up from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store through the instance role.
3. Make that version the default and delete the old ones.

#### AEC-014: Credential in a Lambda function's environment variables

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Lambda functions and function URLs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-envvars.html#configuration-envvars-encryption)

Anyone who can read the function's configuration, including read-only roles and tools like this one, sees the value in clear text. It's also copied into every version of the function.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential.
2. Store it in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store and read it at start-up through the function's role.
3. Remove the variable and publish a new version.

#### ACN-005: Credential in an ECS task definition's environment variables

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** ECS services and their task definitions (environment variables scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/secrets-envvar-secrets-manager.html)

Task definitions are readable by anyone who can describe them, in every revision ever registered, so the credential is in clear text for every read-only role and tool.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential.
2. Store it in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.
3. Register a revision that passes it under secrets (valueFrom) instead of environment, and deregister the old revisions.

#### AIM-004: Credential stored inside an image

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning, ECR images: tags, digests, and when each was pushed and last pulled, Pulling ECR images, for Trivy to scan, Packages, vulnerabilities and stored credentials in container images (Aqua Trivy) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/specifying-sensitive-data.html)

Anyone who can pull the image can read the credential, from every copy of the image in every registry and cache, for as long as those exist. Deleting the file in a later layer doesn't remove it from the earlier one.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential: treat it as leaked.
2. Remove it from the build: pass secrets at run time (the platform's secret store) or with a build secret mount, and add the file to .dockerignore.
3. Rebuild, deploy, and delete the old image tags.

#### ASC-001: Secret's resource policy lets anyone read it

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Secrets Manager secrets (names and dates, never values) and their resource policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/auth-and-access_resource-policies.html)

Its resource policy allows "*" without a condition, so any AWS account can read the secret's value.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the secret now.
2. In Secrets Manager → the secret → Resource permissions, remove the statement for "*", or name the accounts and roles that need it. Secrets Manager's Block public policy option refuses such statements in future.

#### ASC-002: Secret hasn't changed in over a year

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Secrets Manager secrets (names and dates, never values) and their resource policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotating-secrets.html)

The same value has been in use for more than a year, so anyone who copied it at any point in that time, a former employee or a leaked log, can still use it.

**How to fix**

Turn on rotation in Secrets Manager → the secret → Rotation, with a rotation function for databases and AWS services. For a third party's API key, issue a new key, store it, and revoke the old one.

#### ASC-003: Secret unused for 90 days

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Secrets Manager secrets (names and dates, never values) and their resource policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/manage_delete-secret.html)

Nothing has read the secret in three months, so it most likely guards something no longer in use, while the credential itself still works.

**How to fix**

Find out what it was for. Revoke the credential at its source, then delete the secret in Secrets Manager (it can be restored during the recovery window).

#### ASC-004: KMS key policy lets anyone use the key

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** KMS keys, their rotation and key policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html)

The key policy allows "*" without a condition, so other AWS accounts can decrypt data encrypted with it, or use it to encrypt yours.

**How to fix**

In KMS → the key → Key policy → Edit, replace the "*" principal with your account and the roles that use the key, or add a condition (aws:PrincipalOrgID, kms:CallerAccount).

#### ASC-005: KMS key doesn't rotate automatically

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** KMS keys, their rotation and key policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html)

The same key material encrypts everything for as long as the key exists. Yearly rotation limits how much data any one version of the key protects, at no cost to existing data.

**How to fix**

In KMS → the key → Key rotation, turn on Automatically rotate this KMS key (every 365 days, or a shorter period).

#### ASC-008: Credential in a CodeBuild project

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** CodeBuild projects (environment variables scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-env-ref-env-vars.html)

A plain-text environment variable or a source URL with a password in it is readable by anyone who can view the project, and shows in build logs.

**How to fix**

1. Rotate the credential.
2. Store it in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store and reference it with the SECRETS_MANAGER or PARAMETER_STORE variable type.
3. Connect the source with a CodeConnections connection instead of a URL with a password.

### AWS: TLS & HTTPS

#### ADB-005: Database accepts connections without TLS

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** RDS databases, RDS parameters that require TLS · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/UsingWithRDS.SSL.html)

Clients may connect in plain text, so passwords and query results cross the network unencrypted, and anyone on that path can read or change them.

**How to fix**

In the database's parameter group (its cluster parameter group for Aurora), set rds.force_ssl to 1 for PostgreSQL, or require_secure_transport to ON for MySQL and MariaDB, after checking that every client connects with TLS.

#### ADB-008: OpenSearch domain accepts plain HTTP or TLS 1.0

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** OpenSearch domains · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/infrastructure-security.html)

Clients can send queries and credentials in plain text or over an old TLS version that can be broken.

**How to fix**

In OpenSearch → the domain → Actions → Edit, under Encryption, turn on Require HTTPS for all traffic and choose a TLS security policy with TLS 1.2 as the minimum.

#### ADB-009: Cache accepts unencrypted connections

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** ElastiCache clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/in-transit-encryption.html)

Whatever the cache holds (sessions, tokens, cached query results) crosses the network in plain text.

**How to fix**

Modify the cluster to turn on encryption in transit, first in preferred mode while clients move to TLS, then in required mode.

#### AMQ-002: SNS delivers messages over plain HTTP

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** SNS topics, their policies and subscriptions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-http-https-endpoint-as-subscriber.html)

Messages, and any data in them, cross the internet unencrypted to the subscriber, where anyone on the path can read or change them.

**How to fix**

Subscribe the endpoint again with an https:// URL, confirm the new subscription, and delete the http one.

#### AED-001: CloudFront distribution serves plain HTTP

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html)

Visitors who arrive over HTTP stay on HTTP, so anyone on their network can read or change what they see, including session cookies.

**How to fix**

In CloudFront → the distribution → Behaviors, edit each behavior and set Viewer protocol policy to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

#### AED-002: CloudFront distribution accepts TLS 1.0 or 1.1

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/secure-connections-supported-viewer-protocols-ciphers.html)

TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known weaknesses and are no longer accepted by PCI DSS or current browsers. Accepting them lets an attacker downgrade a visitor's connection.

**How to fix**

In CloudFront → the distribution → Settings → Edit, set Security policy to TLSv1.2_2021 or newer.

#### AED-004: CloudFront reaches its origin over plain HTTP

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-cloudfront-to-custom-origin.html)

The visitor sees a padlock, but the request travels unencrypted between CloudFront and the origin, where it can be read or altered.

**How to fix**

Install a certificate on the origin, then in CloudFront → the distribution → Origins, edit the origin and set Protocol to HTTPS only.

#### AED-005: Load balancer serves plain HTTP

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-listeners.html#redirect-actions)

The internet-facing load balancer answers on HTTP without sending visitors to HTTPS, so their requests and cookies cross the network unencrypted.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Load Balancers → the load balancer → Listeners, edit the HTTP listener's default action to Redirect to HTTPS on port 443.

#### AED-006: Load balancer accepts TLS 1.0 or 1.1

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/describe-ssl-policies.html)

The listener's security policy still negotiates TLS 1.0 or 1.1, which have known weaknesses and fail PCI DSS.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Load Balancers → the load balancer → Listeners, edit the HTTPS listener and choose the recommended policy, ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 or newer.

#### AED-011: Certificate in use won't renew and is about to expire

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** ACM certificates · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/check-certificate-renewal-status.html)

The certificate is imported, or ACM can't renew it, so when it expires every load balancer, distribution or API that uses it stops working for visitors.

**How to fix**

For an imported certificate, get a new one from its issuer and reimport it under the same ARN. For an ACM certificate, fix what blocks renewal (usually the DNS validation record) in ACM → the certificate → Renewal status.

#### AED-012: IAM server certificate has expired

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** IAM server certificates · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_server-certs.html)

An expired certificate still attached to a load balancer or distribution breaks HTTPS for its visitors, and an old one left in IAM can be attached again by mistake.

**How to fix**

Move whatever uses it to a certificate from ACM, which renews itself, then delete it with aws iam delete-server-certificate.

### AWS: WAF & bots

#### AED-003: CloudFront distribution has no web ACL

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/distribution-web-awswaf.html)

Requests reach the application behind the distribution without AWS WAF looking at them: no managed rules for common attacks, no rate limits, no bot control.

**How to fix**

In CloudFront → the distribution → Security, enable AWS WAF protections. Start with the core managed rules and a rate limit. If another WAF sits in front of this distribution (Cloudflare, for example), mark this as accepted.

#### AED-007: Internet-facing application load balancer has no web ACL

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners, WAF web ACLs, their logging and what they protect, CloudFront distributions · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/web-acl-associating-aws-resource.html)

Requests reach the application with nothing filtering common attacks, bad bots or floods from single addresses, and no way to block an address quickly during an incident.

**How to fix**

In WAF & Shield → Web ACLs, create a web ACL in the load balancer's region with AWS's managed core rule set and a rate-based rule, and associate it with the load balancer. A distribution with a web ACL in front of it, and the load balancer locked to CloudFront, also works.

#### AED-008: WAF web ACL has no rules

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** WAF web ACLs, their logging and what they protect · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/web-acl-editing.html)

The web ACL is in place but has no rules, so it only applies its default action to everything: it looks like protection and filters nothing.

**How to fix**

In WAF & Shield → Web ACLs → the web ACL → Rules → Add rules, add AWS's managed core rule set and known bad inputs rule set, and a rate-based rule.

#### XP-006: Origin behind Cloudflare accepts traffic from the whole internet

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Spans providers** · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners, Security groups, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs · [Cloudflare docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/security/protect-your-origin-server/)

Visitors reach this origin through Cloudflare, where your WAF, rate limits and bot rules run. Its security group also lets anyone connect to it directly, and origin addresses are easy to find (certificate logs, old DNS records, internet scans). An attacker who connects directly skips every Cloudflare protection and can flood the origin itself.

**How to fix**

1. In the security group, replace 0.0.0.0/0 on ports 80 and 443 with Cloudflare's address ranges (cloudflare.com/ips); a managed prefix list keeps them in one place.
2. Or connect the origin through Cloudflare Tunnel and remove the inbound rule altogether.
3. Turn on Authenticated Origin Pulls in Cloudflare so the origin can refuse requests that didn't come through your zone.

### AWS: DNS

#### ADN-001: Route 53 record points at an AWS resource the entity doesn't have

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Route 53 hosted zones and records, CloudFront distributions, S3 buckets, Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/protection-from-dangling-dns.html)

The record names a CloudFront distribution, load balancer or S3 bucket that none of the entity's AWS accounts has. A missing bucket or CloudFront alias can be claimed by anyone, who then serves content under your hostname. A missing load balancer can't be claimed (its name is random), so that record is dead, or points into an AWS account Keelson doesn't see.

**How to fix**

1. If the site was retired, delete the record in Route
2. If it should be live, recreate the resource or point the record at the current one.
3. If the resource belongs to an AWS account that isn't in Keelson, add that account to this entity, or mark the finding as a false positive.

#### ADN-002: Route 53 record points at an AWS address the entity released

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Route 53 hosted zones and records, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/protection-from-dangling-dns.html)

Keelson saw this address in one of the entity's AWS accounts on an earlier scan, and it is gone now: the instance was stopped or deleted, or the Elastic IP was released. AWS hands released addresses to other customers, and whoever gets this one receives your hostname's traffic and can obtain a certificate for it.

**How to fix**

1. If the server is gone, delete the record in Route
2. If it moved, point the record at its current address, and use an Elastic IP or an alias to a load balancer so the address can't change again.
3. If the address moved to an AWS account that isn't in Keelson, add that account to this entity.

#### ADN-003: Route 53 record points at an AWS address outside the entity's accounts

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Route 53 hosted zones and records, Network interfaces and Elastic IPs, AWS's published address ranges (ip-ranges.amazonaws.com) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/protection-from-dangling-dns.html)

The address is in AWS's EC2 range, but none of the entity's AWS accounts holds it. It may be a vendor's server or an AWS account of yours that Keelson doesn't scan. It may also be an address you released before Keelson started watching, which AWS has since given to someone else.

**How to fix**

1. Find out who runs the server at that address.
2. If it is an AWS account of yours, add it to this entity so its addresses are tracked.
3. If it is a vendor's, mark the finding as accepted.
4. If nobody knows, delete the record.

#### XP-005: Route 53 record points at Vercel, but no Vercel project in the entity serves it

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Spans providers** · **Reads:** Route 53 hosted zones and records · [Vercel docs](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain)

The record sends visitors to Vercel, yet none of the entity's Vercel projects has this hostname. Whoever adds it to their own Vercel project first serves your traffic under your domain.

**How to fix**

1. If the site moved or was retired, delete the record in Route
2. If it should be live, add the hostname to the right Vercel project under Settings → Domains.
3. If it belongs to a Vercel team that isn't in Keelson, add that team to this entity, or mark the finding as a false positive.

#### XP-021: Route 53 record points at an Alibaba Cloud resource or address the entity doesn't have

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Spans providers** · **Reads:** Route 53 hosted zones and records · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/map-custom-domain-names-5)

The record names an OSS bucket, load balancer or CDN domain that none of the entity's Alibaba Cloud accounts has, or an address Keelson saw leave them. Alibaba Cloud hands released addresses to other customers, and a deleted bucket's name can be registered again, so someone else may answer for your hostname.

**How to fix**

1. If the site moved or was retired, delete the record in Route
2. If it should be live, recreate the resource or point the record at the current one.
3. If the resource belongs to an Alibaba Cloud account that isn't in Keelson, add that account to this entity.

### AWS: Platform

#### AEC-001: Instance still allows IMDSv1

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** EC2 instances · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html)

With IMDSv1, a single server-side request forgery bug in anything on the instance hands out the instance role's credentials. IMDSv2 requires a session token that such a bug can't obtain.

**How to fix**

1. Check that the software on the instance uses a current AWS SDK.
2. In EC2 → the instance → Actions → Instance settings → Modify instance metadata options, set IMDSv2 to Required.
3. Set it in your launch templates too, so new instances start that way.

#### AEC-002: EBS volumes aren't encrypted by default

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** EBS encryption, public snapshots and public images, EC2 instances · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/encryption-by-default.html)

New volumes and snapshots in this region are unencrypted unless someone remembers to tick the box, and an unencrypted snapshot can be shared or copied out as it is.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Settings → Data protection and security for the region, turn on Always encrypt new EBS volumes. Existing volumes stay as they are.

#### AEC-005: Lambda function runs on a deprecated runtime

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Lambda functions and function URLs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtimes.html)

AWS has stopped patching this runtime, so vulnerabilities in the language and its libraries stay open, and AWS will eventually block updates to the function.

**How to fix**

Test the function on a supported runtime, then change it under Lambda → the function → Code → Runtime settings → Edit.

#### AEC-009: Launch template allows IMDSv1

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** EC2 launch templates (start-up scripts scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-IMDS-new-instances.html)

Every instance started from it, by an Auto Scaling group or by hand, answers the old metadata service, so a server-side request forgery in its software can read the instance role's credentials.

**How to fix**

Create a new version of the launch template with Metadata version set to V2 only (token required), make it the default, and start an instance refresh on the Auto Scaling groups that use it.

#### AEC-011: EBS volume isn't encrypted

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** EBS volumes · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-encryption.html)

The volume, and every snapshot taken of it, is stored in the clear. An unencrypted snapshot can be shared or copied to another account as it is.

**How to fix**

Volumes can't be encrypted in place. Snapshot the volume, copy the snapshot with encryption on, create a volume from the copy and swap it in. Turn on EBS encryption by default so new volumes are encrypted.

#### ACN-003: EKS cluster runs a Kubernetes version past standard support

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** EKS clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/kubernetes-versions.html)

The version gets security fixes only under extended support, which costs more per cluster hour and ends on a date, after which AWS upgrades the cluster for you. An unsupported version gets no fixes at all.

**How to fix**

Plan the upgrade: check deprecated APIs, upgrade the control plane one minor version at a time in EKS → the cluster → Upgrade version, then the node groups and add-ons.

#### ACN-004: ECS task runs a privileged container or shares the host

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** ECS services and their task definitions (environment variables scanned for credentials, never stored) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html#container_definition_security)

A privileged container, or one in the host's network or process namespace, can reach the host it runs on and every other container there. A compromise of the application becomes a compromise of the host.

**How to fix**

Register a new revision of the task definition without Privileged, and with awsvpc or bridge networking and no host PID or IPC mode. Grant the specific Linux capabilities it needs instead, then update the service to the new revision.

#### ACN-007: ECR images aren't scanned for vulnerabilities

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)

Images are pushed and run without anyone being told they contain packages with known vulnerabilities.

**How to fix**

In ECR → Private registry → Feature & Settings → Scanning, add a rule that scans on push for all repositories (filter *), or turn on enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector.

#### ADB-002: Database storage isn't encrypted

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** RDS databases · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.Encryption.html)

Its disks, automated backups and snapshots are stored in the clear, and an unencrypted snapshot can be shared or copied to another account as it is.

**How to fix**

1. Encryption can't be turned on in place.
2. Take a snapshot.
3. Copy the snapshot with encryption enabled.
4. Restore a new database from the encrypted copy and switch the application to it.

#### ADB-003: Database has no automated backups

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** RDS databases · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups.html)

With retention set to zero there are no daily backups and no point-in-time recovery. A bad migration, a deleted table or ransomware can't be undone.

**How to fix**

In RDS → the database → Modify → Backup, set the backup retention period to at least 7 days.

#### ADB-007: OpenSearch domain doesn't encrypt its data

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** OpenSearch domains · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/encryption-at-rest.html)

Its indexes are stored, or passed between its nodes, in the clear. Fine-grained access control also can't be turned on without both.

**How to fix**

In OpenSearch → the domain → Actions → Edit security configuration, turn on Encryption of data at rest and Node-to-node encryption (on older domains, create a new domain and restore a snapshot).

#### ADB-010: Cache stores data unencrypted

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** ElastiCache clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/at-rest-encryption.html)

Its disk and its backups are stored in the clear.

**How to fix**

Encryption at rest can't be turned on in place: take a backup, create a new cluster with encryption at rest from it, and switch clients over.

#### ADB-012: Redshift cluster isn't encrypted

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Redshift clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/working-with-db-encryption.html)

The warehouse's data and its snapshots are stored in the clear.

**How to fix**

In Redshift → the cluster → Properties → Database configurations → Edit encryption, choose AWS KMS. Redshift migrates the data in place.

#### ADB-013: DynamoDB table can't be restored to a point in time

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** DynamoDB tables and point-in-time recovery · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/PointInTimeRecovery.html)

A bad deployment, a script that deletes the wrong items or a compromised credential can wipe the table, and there is nothing to restore it from.

**How to fix**

In DynamoDB → the table → Backups → Point-in-time recovery, choose Edit and turn it on.

#### ADB-014: EFS file system isn't encrypted

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** EFS file systems · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/encryption.html)

Its files and backups are stored in the clear.

**How to fix**

Encryption can't be turned on in place: create an encrypted file system, copy the data with AWS DataSync, and move the mount targets over.

### AWS: Supply chain

#### AIM-001: Image in use has a vulnerability attackers are exploiting

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning, ECR images: tags, digests, and when each was pushed and last pulled, Pulling ECR images, for Trivy to scan, Packages, vulnerabilities and stored credentials in container images (Aqua Trivy), CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)

A package in the image has a vulnerability on CISA's list of known exploited vulnerabilities (cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog), and something runs the image. Attackers already have working exploits for it, and a service the internet reaches is where they try them first.

**How to fix**

1. Rebuild the image with the fixed versions: update the base image for operating system packages, and the lock file for the application's own dependencies (the Images page says which is which).
2. Push it and deploy the workloads that run it.
3. Where there is no fix yet, limit who can reach the workload until there is.

#### AIM-002: Image in use has critical or high vulnerabilities with a fix

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning, ECR images: tags, digests, and when each was pushed and last pulled, Pulling ECR images, for Trivy to scan, Packages, vulnerabilities and stored credentials in container images (Aqua Trivy) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)

The image runs with packages that have known critical or high vulnerabilities, and fixed versions exist. Each rebuild that doesn't pick them up leaves a known way in for longer.

**How to fix**

1. Rebuild the image with the fixed versions: update the base image for operating system packages, and the lock file for the application's own dependencies (the Images page says which is which).
2. Push it and deploy the workloads that run it.
3. Where there is no fix yet, limit who can reach the workload until there is.

#### AIM-003: Image in use is built on an operating system or runtime past its end of life

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning, ECR images: tags, digests, and when each was pushed and last pulled, Pulling ECR images, for Trivy to scan, Packages, vulnerabilities and stored credentials in container images (Aqua Trivy) · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html)

The operating system release in the image, or the release line of the runtime it is built around (Node.js, Python, nginx…), no longer gets security fixes. Vulnerabilities found in it from now on stay open, and scanners stop reporting them for it.

**How to fix**

Change the Dockerfile's FROM line to a release that is still supported (or to the newest tag of the same base image), rebuild, test and deploy.

### AWS: Monitoring

#### ACN-002: EKS cluster keeps no audit log

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** EKS clusters · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/control-plane-logs.html)

There is no record of who called the Kubernetes API: who read a secret, started a pod or changed a role binding. After an incident you can't tell what happened.

**How to fix**

In EKS → the cluster → Observability → Control plane logging → Manage, turn on Audit (and Authenticator). The logs go to CloudWatch Logs; set a retention period on the log group.

#### AMO-001: GuardDuty is off in a region that runs workloads

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** GuardDuty detectors, EC2 instances, RDS databases, Load balancers and listeners, Lambda functions and function URLs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_settingup.html)

Nothing watches the region for stolen credentials in use, instances talking to known malware hosts, or unusual API calls. A compromise there goes unnoticed until the bill or a customer reveals it.

**How to fix**

Open GuardDuty in the region and choose Get started → Enable GuardDuty. With several accounts, enable it for the organization from the delegated administrator account.

#### AMO-002: VPC with running resources has no flow logs

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** VPCs and flow logs, EC2 instances, RDS databases, Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html)

Without flow logs there is no record of which addresses talked to what. After an incident you can't tell what an attacker reached or what data left.

**How to fix**

In the VPC console, select the VPC → Flow logs → Create flow log. Capture rejected traffic at least, and send it to CloudWatch Logs or S3.

#### AMO-003: Internet-facing load balancer keeps no access logs

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** Load balancers and listeners · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/enable-access-logging.html)

The load balancer is where the internet meets your application, and without access logs there is no record of who requested what. After an attack you can't tell which addresses were involved or what they reached.

**How to fix**

In EC2 → Load Balancers → the load balancer → Attributes → Edit, turn on Access logs and choose an S3 bucket. Give the bucket a lifecycle rule so old logs expire.

#### AMO-004: CloudTrail doesn't record every region

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** CloudTrail trails · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/receive-cloudtrail-log-files-from-multiple-regions.html)

API calls in the regions no trail covers aren't kept anywhere beyond 90 days of event history. Attackers often work in regions nobody uses, to start instances or create keys, precisely because nobody looks there.

**How to fix**

In CloudTrail → Trails → Create trail, create one trail that applies to all regions and logs management events, or an organization trail from the management account. Make sure it is logging.

#### AMO-005: CloudTrail log files can't be checked for tampering

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** CloudTrail trails · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html)

Without log file validation, someone who reaches the log bucket can change or delete entries, and nothing shows that the record of their activity was altered.

**How to fix**

In CloudTrail → the trail → General details → Edit, turn on Log file validation.

#### AMO-006: AWS Config isn't recording in a region that runs workloads

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** AWS Config recorders, EC2 instances, RDS databases, Load balancers and listeners, Lambda functions and function URLs · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/gs-console.html)

There is no history of how resources were configured. After an incident you can't tell when a security group opened, a bucket became public or a role changed.

**How to fix**

In AWS Config → Settings, turn on recording for the region (all resource types, or the ones you care about), or deploy it to every account and region with a conformance pack or Control Tower.

#### AMO-007: WAF web ACL doesn't log requests

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** WAF web ACLs, their logging and what they protect · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/logging.html)

There is no record of which requests the web ACL blocked or let through, so an attack it missed, or a rule that blocks real users, goes unnoticed.

**How to fix**

In WAF & Shield → Web ACLs → the web ACL → Logging and metrics, enable logging to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose. Redact headers that carry credentials.

### AWS: Change risk

#### ACN-008: ECR image tags can be overwritten

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** ECR repositories, their policies and image scanning · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-tag-mutability.html)

Anyone who can push can replace the image behind a tag a service already runs, such as a release tag, and the next deployment or restart picks it up with no change anyone reviewed.

**How to fix**

In ECR → the repository → Edit, set Tag immutability to Immutable (with exclusions for tags like latest if you need them), and deploy by digest or by release tag.

#### ASC-006: KMS key is scheduled for deletion

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** KMS keys, their rotation and key policies · [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/deleting-keys.html)

When the waiting period ends, the key is gone and every piece of data encrypted with it (volumes, snapshots, objects, database storage) can never be decrypted again.

**How to fix**

If anything may still use the key, cancel the deletion in KMS → the key → Key actions → Cancel key deletion, and disable it instead while you check its CloudTrail usage.

## Alibaba Cloud

### Alibaba Cloud: Attack surface

#### LOS-001: OSS Block Public Access is off for the account

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** OSS Block Public Access for the account, OSS buckets · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/block-public-access)

Without the account-wide block, any bucket can be made public by one ACL or policy change, now or later. With it on, a mistake on a single bucket can't expose data.

**How to fix**

In the OSS console → Block Public Access (on the overview page), turn it on for the account. Buckets that must be public (a static site, for example) are better served through CDN with origin fetch from a private bucket.

#### LOS-002: OSS bucket is public

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** OSS Block Public Access for the account, OSS buckets, OSS bucket ACLs and Block Public Access, OSS bucket policies (reduced to who they allow, never stored) · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/oss-bucket-acl)

Anyone on the internet can list and download the bucket's objects, with no record of who did. Public buckets are the most common source of leaked data in object storage, because whatever is uploaded later is public too. A bucket anyone can also write to can be filled with malware served from your name, overwritten or emptied, and runs up your bill.

**How to fix**

1. If the bucket shouldn't be public, open it in OSS → Permission Control and turn on Block Public Access.
2. Set its ACL to private and remove statements that allow "*" from its bucket policy.
3. If it serves a website, put CDN in front with private origin fetch, then make the bucket private.

#### LOS-003: OSS bucket has no Block Public Access of its own

**Severity:** Low · **Reads:** OSS Block Public Access for the account, OSS buckets, OSS bucket ACLs and Block Public Access · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/block-public-access)

The bucket is private today, but neither it nor the account blocks public access, so one ACL or policy change makes it public.

**How to fix**

1. If the bucket serves a website or downloads through Alibaba Cloud CDN, turn on access to private OSS buckets in the CDN domain's origin settings, then make the bucket private.
2. Otherwise set its ACL to private and remove the policy statement for "*".
3. Then turn on Block Public Access for the bucket, in OSS → the bucket → Permission Control.

#### LNW-001: Security group opens SSH or RDP to the internet

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Security groups and their rules, Network interfaces and EIPs · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/security-group-rules)

Remote administration ports are scanned and brute-forced around the clock. An exposed SSH or RDP port turns one weak password or unpatched service into a foothold.

**How to fix**

1. Edit the group's inbound rules and replace 0.0.0.0/0 with your office or VPN range.
2. Better: remove the rule and connect with Session Manager (Workbench) or Cloud Assistant, which need no inbound port.
3. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### LNW-002: Security group opens a database port to the internet

**Severity:** High · **Reads:** Security groups and their rules, Network interfaces and EIPs · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/security-group-rules)

A database reachable from the internet is protected by its password alone, and exposed to every bug in its network protocol.

**How to fix**

Edit the group's inbound rules so the database port is allowed only from the security group of the application that uses it, not from 0.0.0.0/0. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### LNW-003: Security group allows all traffic from the internet

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Security groups and their rules, Network interfaces and EIPs · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/security-group-rules)

Every port of everything that uses this group is reachable by anyone: admin interfaces, databases, debug ports and services nobody remembers are listening.

**How to fix**

Edit the group's inbound rules: delete the rule that allows all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, and add rules for the specific ports the service needs. If nothing uses the group, delete it.

#### LNW-005: Internet-facing load balancer forwards an admin or database port to anyone

**Severity:** High · **Attack path** · **Reads:** Load balancers (ALB, NLB, CLB) and listeners · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/slb/classic-load-balancer/user-guide/access-control)

The load balancer passes connections from the whole internet to SSH, RDP or a database behind it. The servers' security groups don't stop it: they must let the load balancer's own addresses in, and the load balancer lets everyone through. This exposure doesn't show in the security groups' rules.

**How to fix**

1. Remove the listener if nothing outside needs the port; reach servers through Workbench or a VPN instead.
2. Otherwise turn on access control for the listener (CLB → the instance → Listener → Access Control) with a whitelist of the addresses that need it, or, for an NLB, attach a security group that allows only those addresses.

#### LNW-004: Instance runs in the classic network

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** ECS instances · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/migrate-ecs-instances-from-the-classic-network-to-a-vpc)

The classic network is shared between Alibaba Cloud customers. Instances on it aren't isolated in a VPC of your own, so other tenants' instances sit on the same network and only security groups stand between them.

**How to fix**

Migrate the instance to a VPC (ECS console → the instance → Migrate to VPC), then check its security groups.

#### LEC-009: Internet-facing Linux instance signs in with a password over SSH

**Severity:** Medium · **Attack path** · **Reads:** ECS instances, Security groups and their rules, Network interfaces and EIPs · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/ssh-key-pairs)

The instance has no SSH key pair, so it was set up to sign in with a password, which Alibaba Cloud's public Linux images accept over SSH. Its security group lets the whole internet reach port 22, where passwords are guessed around the clock, and one weak or reused password is a shell on the server.

**How to fix**

1. In the ECS console → the instance → Bind Key Pair, attach an SSH key pair: Alibaba Cloud then turns password sign-in off on its Linux images.
2. Restrict port 22 to your office or VPN range, or remove it and connect with Workbench or Cloud Assistant, which need no inbound port.

#### LEC-008: Custom image is shared outside the entity

**Severity:** Medium · **Reads:** Custom images and who they're shared with · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/share-a-custom-image)

Whoever the image is shared with can start an instance from it and read everything on its disks: application code, configuration, and any credential that was on the server when the image was made.

**How to fix**

1. If the account is yours, add it to this entity in Keelson.
2. Otherwise open the image in ECS → Images → Share Image and remove the account, or stop sharing it with everyone.

#### LDB-001: Database whitelist admits every address

**Severity:** Critical · **Attack path** · **Reads:** ApsaraDB RDS instances, their whitelists, TLS and encryption · [Alibaba Cloud docs](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/rds/apsaradb-rds-for-mysql/configure-an-ip-address-whitelist-for-an-apsaradb-rds-for-mysql-instance)

ApsaraDB instances (RDS, Tair and MongoDB) accept connections only from the addresses in their whitelist. This one admits 0.0.0.0/0, so with a public endpoint anyone on the internet can try its passwords and its protocol's bugs; without one, every host that can reach the network can.

**How to fix**

1. In the instance's console → Whitelist Settings, replace 0.0.0.0/0 with the addresses or security groups of the applications that connect.
2. Release the public endpoint if nothing outside Alibaba Cloud needs it.
